blocks.text: It Started With a Simple Question
What do you do when you want to get out and experience something new, but can't think of anywhere to go?

I can't count the number of times I've stood in the living room trying to figure out where to go and what to do. Nothing I came up with seemed quite right. The idea would take too long, it was too expensive, or it was outside. The Pacific Northwest has a habit of putting a damper on your outdoor activities nine months a year. And when we did get out, the photos ended up buried in my phone.

I needed something that would just give me ideas. Ideas that didn't get boring or repetitive, or take too long when I only had a few hours. I bought a few books, a few card packs, and subscribed to a few adventure catalogs. Most of them didn't feel like they were made for me. And even when one was close, it was too easy to turn it down and flip to the next idea, which sounded just as bad in my head. I knew then that if I wanted something that worked, I would have to build it.
If I Want It, I'll Build It: The Process of Overthinking

Over the next few days I came up with roughly thirty ideas that I kept in a list on my phone. Now all I needed was a way to hand them out. Picking one from a list I could see all of wasn't it either. I'd just compare them and talk myself out of every one. I needed a little magic. Hundreds of ways to deliver adventures came to mind, and I made a list of those too. But I couldn't decide. Do I throw the ideas in a randomizer? Do I put them all in a jar? Neither sounded quite right, and honestly, I needed a project to carry me through the winter.

Each idea was as good as the last, and each took a wildly different amount of effort. So I set down my phone, turned off my computer and went to bed. Lying there, I remembered what my siblings and I used to do when we couldn't decide on something.
Consult the Magic 8 Ball: A Lesson in Simplicity

Shake it, flip it, wait for the little triangle to float up. That was how my siblings and I settled every argument we couldn't settle ourselves. It never gave us a list to argue over. It gave us one answer, and that was the end of it. And who am I to argue with a 75-year-old toy that still sells a million a year?
The simplicity of randomness was the perfect method after all.

That was the trick. The 8 Ball never showed us the other answers, so there was nothing to compare and nothing to talk ourselves out of. That's what was wrong with the books and the card packs: I could see everything, so I'd pick everything apart. So I hid the list. My first version rolled a die, and soon after, I swapped it for a sealed envelope. Open it, and one mission slides out like a letter meant just for you. No list, no second-guessing, just go. And if I was going to spend the whole winter building this thing, it seemed a shame to keep it to myself. I wanted my friends to be able to open one too. I'd never built anything like it, but how hard could it be?
Ridiculously Hard: A Comedy of Errors

I had built websites before, but I was not ready for the chaos of hand-coding one instead of using a website builder like Squarespace. There's no drag-and-drop when you're writing every line yourself. Every button, every color, every bit of spacing is something you decided, which also means every broken thing is something you broke.

And I broke a *lot*. The first version looked horrible. Not "rough around the edges" horrible, but "what the hell were you thinking" horrible. I'd fix one thing on a computer, check my phone and find three new problems. In the first week alone I fixed the same form link half a dozen times, chased down a little icon that refused to load, and renumbered the missions twice because they kept coming out wrong. At one point a whole batch of map pins was broken because I'd missed a single comma. One comma.

After many, *many* late nights, I was finally getting comfortable with the site, and my list of features grew faster than the website did: filters for everything, maps, accounts, ratings, a dozen ways to sort and browse. Every idea sounded like the one that would make it great. But the more I added, the more I drifted from the 8 Ball. A page full of options is just the card pack all over again, with more buttons, more confusion, and more regret. So I cut.
The Art of Deleting Things

I must have cut back a third of the site, and it was already pretty bare to begin with, so it felt like a massive step backwards. But after what was basically Ctrl+A, Delete, I sat back and saw the way through.

I was trying, and failing, to build the way everyone builds. And I don't have an if-you-can't-beat-'em-join-'em mentality. I would lean on my own weirdness, and for some reason, that really worked for AmbleBee. I didn't want the same white backgrounds, gray boxes and feeds that never end. I wanted AmbleBee to feel like something tucked away in a scrapbook. So I made it warm: oat-colored paper, sage greens, honey yellows, and a little bee wandering down her trail. Don't ask me why bees. It was 4 a.m., and I'm pretty sure I was hallucinating.

Adventures became missions, and missions became a love letter to yourself. No posts, no endless scrolling. One click, and a card opens. Sending one to a friend is just as easy, with a wax seal and a note tucked safely inside.
Trust Me: I Checked Every Pin

Apparently, cutting back a third of the website only gave me more room to make a mess. Thirty missions turned into over 300, with a pack started for every state in the country. And somehow, it was only October.

With over 300 missions on the site, I filtered down to Oregon, picked a mission and headed out. I made my way to the pin on the mission card and looked around. Absolutely nothing. And when I say nothing, I mean the road ended. There was supposed to be a lake here.
There is no lake.
I wandered around for nearly half an hour, peering through the trees, hoping to catch a glimpse of water. Nothing. Apparently I'd managed to lose an entire lake.

Remember the scene in *The Princess Bride* where Miracle Max says there's a big difference between mostly dead and all dead? That was my phone. Mostly dead, and getting closer to all dead with every minute of GPS. Halfway home, it finally gave up, and it took me twice as long to find my way back.

When I finally got home, I pulled up Google Maps to figure out where I'd gone wrong. The lake was right where it was supposed to be. My map pin, however, was almost four miles east. One wrong digit buried in the decimal places of the coordinates had sent me on a very different adventure.
I corrected the pin, saved the mission, and sat back. If one wrong number could send me four miles into the middle of nowhere, how many more had I missed?

I knew what I had to do. Every mission had to come down and be checked again, this time properly. That night it was Ctrl+A, Delete all over again, only this time it was 346 missions instead of a third of the site.
Measure Twice, Publish Once

The next morning, the site was basically empty. Nearly two weeks of work, sitting in drafts. I decided that if I was going to continue, there would have to be one rule: a mission only comes back once I'd send my own family there.

That meant checking everything by hand. I spent countless hours staring at satellite imagery, digging through park websites, government pages, AllTrails, and travel blogs. Every pin, every address, every website, tag, theme, caution and description needed checking. One by one, I brought the drafts back from the Pit of Despair. Some map pins moved a few feet, while others moved miles. Not one of them was going to leave someone staring at a lake that isn't there.

And since my phone had already taught me one lesson the hard way, the missions learned it too. If a place has spotty or no cell service, the mission card tells you before you leave, so you can download a map, charge up, or at least tell someone where you're headed. Other heads-ups landed on the cards as well: things worth knowing before you go, so the only surprise on a mission is a good one. No more dead phones at the end of a dead-end road.

But even after all that checking, I knew I could still miss something. A typo, a misplaced pin, a website that stopped working. So I did what I always do when I find a problem: I built something to catch it. First came a checker to make sure Amble Anywhere missions could actually be done anywhere. Then a pin checker to flag coordinates that didn't match their destinations, and another to test every website linked on the mission cards. None of them replaced the hours of research. They're just one last safety net before a mistake makes it out into the world.

Then I noticed something else. Oregon's mission pack was almost entirely hikes. Beautiful hikes, sure, but it rains here for what feels like nine months of the year. What good is a pack full of adventures if half the time you don't want to do any of them?

And Oregon wasn't the only problem. Some states had almost nothing inexpensive, others were missing indoor activities or date ideas. I was so focused on making sure every mission was somewhere worth going that I'd forgotten to make sure there was something for everyone.

So I built another tool. Mission Management became my little workshop for keeping the packs balanced: dates and adventures, indoor and outdoor, cheap and expensive. It shows me where the gaps are, so I can spend less time guessing what to add next and more time finding places worth sharing. It's a tool that keeps me from overthinking, which, if you've read this far, you know I desperately need.
It Takes a Hive: Friends, Strangers and a Front Door

Even with the new tools, there were still hundreds of missions to research, write, and check. I needed help. And as it turns out, friends will do a surprising amount of work for mid-tier pizza. So I conned a few of them into team editing nights: missions spread across the screen, arguing over wording, double-checking opening hours and laughing at some of the stranger places the old pins had wandered off to.
One at a time, the missions came back. Today there are 378 of them live on AmbleBee, and every single one was measured twice.

Then something I didn't expect started to happen. Friends started telling their friends. Those friends told theirs. Before long, people I'd never met were sending me their favorite places: [Blue Pool](https://amblebee.com/missions/blue-pool-hike/), with the coldest water I've ever touched, the stunning rock formation that is [Mobius Arch](https://amblebee.com/missions/mobius-arch-alabama-hills/), and a concert under the stars at [Red Rocks Amphitheatre](https://amblebee.com/missions/red-rocks-amphitheatre/). That's exactly what I'd hoped AmbleBee would become.

There was just one problem. Every one of those ideas came in through a plain Google Form that looked nothing like the rest of the site. Once someone hit Submit, their idea vanished into a spreadsheet, and they never heard what happened to it. If a stranger took the time to share a place they love, they deserved better than a void.

So on November 12, I built AmbleBee a front door. Now when you suggest a mission, report a problem or just say hi, it comes straight to me in AmbleBee's own inbox. You get a private link to follow along. You can watch your idea go from Received to In review, then Working on it, and finally Live, with your name on the mission if you'd like the credit. If I have a question, I can ask it right there, and you can answer without digging through your email.

The whole thing runs on a personally managed server, not on some giant company's cloud. That matters to me. What you send stays with AmbleBee, and it's looked after: your name and email are removed automatically 90 days after your suggestion goes live or is closed, and everything is backed up every night.
What started as a better suggestion box quietly became the heart of AmbleBee. It's where your ideas land, where your problems get fixed, and soon, where a lot more will live.
Something to Come Back To

For a while, AmbleBee did one thing well: it handed you a mission. You'd open an envelope, go have an adventure, and that was it. But I kept thinking about what happened after. You'd come home with a camera roll full of photos and a great story, and AmbleBee had no idea you'd even gone. There was nothing to show for it.

So on November 16, missions got a **Mark done** button. Tap it when you get home, give the mission a thumbs up or down, and jot down anything you want to remember. Every few missions, a stamp lands in your own stamp book. Some are milestones, some show up for the seasons, and a few are surprises I won't spoil here. I care a lot about those stamps, so your profile keeps them safe on any device. No name, no password, just a private link that's yours.

The next day, missions learned to wait for you. Pick one you like, tap **Add to calendar** and send it to whichever calendar you use. After the day passes, AmbleBee asks a simple question: *did you go?*

Then came my favorite. Deciding where to go as a group is its own special kind of torture. Everyone says "I don't care," and then cares a whole lot. So now you can start a vote: pick a few missions, send your friends the link, and let everyone weigh in. The winner lands on a podium, ready to add to everyone's calendar. If you think about it, it's the Magic 8 Ball all over again, just with more people shaking it.

And then, of course, I did it again. With every new feature, the homepage got a little busier. A button here, a filter there, until opening AmbleBee felt more like reading a menu than opening a letter. So I went back to the lesson that started all of this. On November 22, the homepage got one big button: **Give me a mission**. Everything else is still there, just a tap away, but the first thing you see is the same thing the 8 Ball always gave us: one answer, and a little magic.
Oh, and a place to tell stories like this one. You're reading it.
The Part I Haven't Told You
AmbleBee was never supposed to be just a website.

Somewhere in the middle of those first thirty missions, I got a little carried away. What started as a way to hand out adventures turned into the idea for a little camera. You'd pick it up, and its screen would show you a mission. You would go and do it, take your photos, and when you got home, you would set the camera on the dock beside a frame on your wall. Your photos would land right there, next to the mission they came from. No SD cards, no digging through your phone, no "I'll sort these later." Just the adventures and the memories, together.
It was a lovely idea. It was also a *ridiculously* ambitious place to start.

So I scaled back. Before spending a year or more building hardware, I wanted to know if anyone would even enjoy the missions. A little website seemed like a good way to find out. Somewhere along the way, that little test became something much bigger, and I’m glad it did.

But it’s still teaching me. Every mission you open, every stamp you collect, every vote you start shows me what the Hive should become. Because the Hive isn’t just a picture frame. It’s a place for your adventures to live after you’ve had them.

The next step is to bring those experiences off the screen and onto your wall. With **the Hive**, you'll be able to pick a mission, go do it, and send your photos to the frame with a QR code. No app, no account, no cloud. Each completed mission becomes a little memory, with its photos and a note. And after that comes AmbleCam, the camera that helped inspire the whole thing. It already takes pictures on my workbench, so it's not just a dream, just a lot of wires waiting their turn.

Until then, there's plenty to do. [Suggest a mission](https://amblebee.com/suggest/) you love, [vote in a poll](https://amblebee.com/contribute/) on the Contribute page, or follow along on the [Bee trail](https://amblebee.com/roadmap.html) to see what's coming next.
So the next time you're standing in the living room with no idea where to go, you know who to ask.

posts.summary: A Magic 8 Ball, a lake that wasn’t there, and 346 missions I had to take down. Here’s how AmbleBee went from a list on my phone to something people actually use.
posts.title: AmbleBee: A Developing Story

blocks.text:
Greetings, valued ~~data source~~ human.

Here at AmbleBee, your privacy is of the utmost importance to us. After all, it's how we ~~generate shareholder value~~ build a better experience.

Please remain calm as we outline our ambitious plans to ~~monetize your personal information~~ make AmbleBee the best it can be.

As always, we remain committed to putting our ~~shareholders~~ users first.

We thank you for your continued ~~compliance~~ support.

— The AmbleBee Board of Directors
I Don't Want Your Data.
Normally, that is a pretty good sign that someone does, in fact, want your data. But here at AmbleBee, we do things differently. And if you trust me when I say that, you probably shouldn't.

Many of the major companies we trust with our personal information, whether that be documents, photos, or otherwise, have publicly stated that they don't sell our personal data. And for the most part, I believe them. What they sell is something arguably more valuable: a way to advertise directly to us.
In 2025, Google and Meta alone brought in nearly half a trillion dollars in advertising revenue. That's roughly $1.35 billion per day. Every day.

No, I'm not going to pretend that I'm not curious about the people who use AmbleBee. I spent thirty hours building a button, and I'd quite like to know if anyone actually presses it. But I don't particularly care *who* pressed it, what they had for breakfast, or what they're thinking about buying next Tuesday.

The Board notes that next Tuesday's purchases represent a ~~revenue opportunity~~ valuable insight.

— The Board
No. Go away.
There is a difference between wanting to understand the people who use your website and wanting to understand how people use your website. And I believe that is the beginning of what sets us apart.

Of course, drawing that line was considerably easier in my head than it was in practice. Every time I built something new, I found myself with another question I wanted answered. Were people actually opening missions? Were they coming back? Was anyone using that feature that I stayed up until two in the morning building?

Each question came with an opportunity to collect a little more information, and each piece of information came with a responsibility I hadn't given much thought to when I started. I needed to decide not only what I wanted to know, but what I was comfortable with knowing.
The Art of Knowing Just Enough

Now, I won't sit here and tell you that I'm smart, because I know for a fact that it's a miracle this website works in the first place. Most of what you see on AmbleBee is the result of trying something, breaking something, and eventually figuring out why. That being said, how do I decide what to collect?
Collect everything, and I'm the problem. Collect nothing, and now I have a problem.
So I sat upon a log in the woods and thought until the thinking stopped.
And what I learned will almost certainly not surprise you: there's a difference between tracking an interaction and tracking an individual.
So how do you track the interaction without the individual?

I did what just about everyone does first. I looked at Google Analytics. It's free, it takes about five minutes to set up, and it'll tell you more about your visitors than you'd ever think to ask. Which, if you remember the half a trillion dollars from earlier, should make you wonder why it's free.

The Board has reviewed Google Analytics and wishes to proceed immediately.

— The Board
Of course they do.

Now, to be fair to Google, it's not as bad as you might think. It doesn't keep your IP address, and plenty of the data it collects is genuinely useful to the people running a website. But the way it knows a visitor came back is a little file it leaves in your browser, a cookie, and [according to Google](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/11397207), its job is to "distinguish users," and it lasts two years. And every time you visit, the two-year clock starts over. Then there's a setting that lets Google use what it collects about your visits to improve its own products. Including its advertising.

The Board would simply like to know if they're coming back. Just that. Nothing else. Probably.

— The Board

Remember my question? Were they coming back? Google Analytics could answer it in a heartbeat. And that was exactly the problem. The only way to know you came back is to remember you, and I don't want to remember you. Not for two years. Not really at all.

So I went looking for another way, and it turns out I wasn't the first person to have this problem. A small analytics company had already figured out a clever way to count visitors without cookies at all. Instead of leaving something in your browser, they make up a new secret every day and use it to scramble a few details about your visit. The same visitor gets the same scramble that day, so you're only counted once. But the next day, the secret's gone, and so are you.
I liked it so much that I built AmbleBee's counter the same way.

Now, I'll be honest: I haven't completely let go of Google Analytics yet. My counter is still new, and I'm still finding the gaps, the things Google can tell me that I can't. So for now, Google Analytics is still on AmbleBee, but only if you say yes. Until you do, it isn't even loaded. And if you do, I've turned off everything I can: no ad personalization, no Google signals, and the detailed data is kept for two months, the shortest option there is. The goal is to learn what's actually worth knowing, build that myself, and then say goodbye to Google for good.

The Board strongly encourages you to opt in. The Board has been very patient.

— The Board

So here's your choice. You can disappoint the Board and stick with my little in-house counter, or give them something to celebrate and opt in to Google Analytics. Either way, you'll get the exact same AmbleBee, the same missions, the same stamps, and no guilt trip from me. Pick whatever you're comfortable with, and if you change your mind, you can switch anytime on the [privacy page](https://amblebee.com/privacy/).
The Board, on the other hand, will absolutely guilt-trip you.
Hello, Stranger

The counter is for people passing through. But some of you don't just pass through. You suggest a place you love, report a pin that sent you somewhere strange, or write in just to say hi. And the moment you do, you stop being a click on a counter and become a person in my inbox.

To do that, I need to know a little about you. If I have a question about the waterfall you suggested, I need a way to ask it. If your idea goes live, you deserve to hear about it, and to see your name on it if you'd like the credit. So for as long as your suggestion is open, your name and email stay with it.

But once it's done, it's done. Ninety days after your suggestion goes live or gets closed, your name and email are removed automatically and replaced with "AmbleBee user," which honestly sounds like witness protection. Old messages in the inbox are deleted on the same clock. And if you'd rather be forgotten sooner, just ask.

The Board proposes keeping all emails forever, for ~~marketing~~ sentimental reasons. This is not a request.

— The Board
The Board doesn't get a vote on this one.
That's the trade. If you suggest another place a year from now, I won't know it's you. I'd rather lose that than keep a list of everyone who ever wrote in, just in case.
Your Computer, Not Mine.

THE BOARD DEMANDS COOKIES.

— The Board
They mean the other kind... They always mean the other kind.

So, sorry to disappoint, but unless you've said yes to Google Analytics, there aren't any. Not one. The only cookies at AmbleBee are the ones my friends eat on team editing nights, and even those got replaced with mid-tier pizza.

That's the thing I learned digging through Google's cookies: a cookie travels. Every time you visit, your browser hands it right back to the website, like showing your ticket at the door. That's how a website knows it's you again.

AmbleBee still remembers things, of course. Your settings, the missions you've marked done, which stamps you've already seen, and your email so you don't have to type it into every form. But all of it lives in a little storage space inside your own browser, and it stays there. It doesn't go anywhere on its own. Your computer remembers you so that I don't have to.

There's just one catch. If you clear your browser, switch phones, or drop your laptop in a lake (assuming you can find one), it's gone. For your settings, that's not a big deal, but for your stamps, or the missions you've marked done, that's heartbreaking.
A Profile With No Name

Stamps are supposed to last. You earn them by actually going places, and losing them to a cleared browser didn't sit right with me. Every other website solves this the same way: make an account. Email, password, maybe a username, and a "forgot password" button, which I'm fairly sure is the most-pressed button on the internet.

Fine. No cookies. The Board would settle for a password. And a security question. And your ~~Social Security number~~ mother's maiden name. Please.

— The Board
Absolutely not.

So AmbleBee profiles don't have a name or a password. Your profile is a private link, and the key inside it is made right there in your browser. AmbleBee only keeps a scrambled version of that key, so even someone holding the whole database couldn't sign in as you. Only your link can.

You can add a recovery email in case you lose your link, but AmbleBee doesn't keep that either. It sends your link once, then holds onto a fingerprint: enough to recognize the address if you type it in again, never enough to read it. The notes you write after a mission are locked before they ever leave your device, so all I could ever see is scrambled text. And if a profile sits empty with nothing marked done, it's deleted after 90 days without a visit.

Of course, there's a catch. If you lose your link and never added a recovery email, I can't get your profile back. There's no account to look up and no password to reset. That's the price of a profile with no name. So if you have stamps worth keeping, add that email.
What I Know About You

All of this runs on a server I manage myself, not on some giant company's cloud. Your suggestions, your profile, the little click counter: they all live in one place, backed up every night, looked after by one person.

And one person can make mistakes. If someone ever broke into the server, I'd want them to walk away disappointed. So here's what they'd find: daily totals from the click counter, scrambled profile keys that can't sign anyone in, notes that are locked so only their owners can read them, and lists of missions marked done, tied to no account and no real identity. Recovery emails are only fingerprints, so nobody could read them, though someone who already knew your email could check whether it's there. Beyond the display names you pick for yourself, the only real names and email addresses on the whole server belong to people with a suggestion or message still open, and even those disappear on the 90-day clock. The nightly backups hold the same things, and they're cleared out after a week, so anything deleted is fully gone about seven days later.

The Board recommends a very large, very expensive security system. With a logo. The Board just wants something.

— The Board
Or we could just not keep much worth stealing.
That's the real reason I don't keep your data. It isn't just that I don't want it. It's that the safest information is the information that was never there in the first place.

To whom it may concern,

Effective immediately, the Board of Directors resigns. We cannot, in good conscience, continue serving a company with no data, no cookies, and no ~~shareholders~~ hope.

— The ~~AmbleBee~~ Former Board of Directors
They'll be back. They always come back, usually right when I'm about to build something new.

I'd love to tell you they're a group of faceless executives in a glass tower somewhere. They aren't. The Board is me, at two in the morning, with a new feature and a bad idea. Every one of their memos was my first thought. Keep the emails. Add the cookies. Find out who's coming back. Building AmbleBee has mostly been learning to say no to myself.
Remember what I said at the beginning? If you trust me when I say we do things differently, you probably shouldn't.

So don't. Check my work. AmbleBee's website is [open source](https://github.com/AmbleBee/amblebee-missions), which means anyone can read exactly what your browser sends me, and what it doesn't. You can see the visit counter for yourself, watch your profile key get made on your own device, and check that your notes are locked before they ever leave it. The server that receives all of it is private, so for that part you'll have to take my word, and the [privacy page](https://amblebee.com/privacy/), which spells out everything AmbleBee keeps and for how long. If any of it ever changes, that page changes first.
So here's what I actually know about you: almost nothing. And that's exactly how I like it.
— Max, Founder, Developer, Mission Checker, and the entire AmbleBee Board of Directors

posts.summary: The AmbleBee Board of Directors has some ambitious plans for your personal information. I have some bad news for the Board.
posts.title: The Board Wants Your Data

blocks.text: ~~At AmbleBee, we're passionate about delivering carefully curated experiences tailored to your unique interests. Our dedicated team works tirelessly to ensure every adventure meets our rigorous quality standards.~~
There is no team. It's me. It's 2 a.m., and I'm on my third energy drink.
Down the Rabbit Hole

Most missions start out one of two ways: with your suggestion or my insanity. Both take time to get just right. Purely for entertainment reasons, let's pick the second route. We'll come back to suggestions in a few minutes.

Crazed research is a learned skill, and one I learned all through high school and college, usually fueled by energy drinks and gas station snacks. My research usually begins with a question: if I had only 24 hours to explore an area of the United States, what would pull at me the most? In the beginning, that was an easy question to answer.

I live in arguably one of the most beautiful and diverse regions in the United States, the Pacific Northwest. Everything I could want is less than a 4-hour drive from my front door, and the rest is well worth the drive, whether that be [Haystack Rock](https://amblebee.com/missions/haystack-rock/) at the coast in the west, the [Alvord Desert](https://amblebee.com/missions/alvord-desert/) in the east, [Mount St. Helens](https://amblebee.com/missions/mount-st-helens/), a volcano up north, or [Wildlife Safari](https://amblebee.com/missions/wildlife-safari/) down south.

I simply started with places I personally wanted to see, or places I had been and would recommend to friends. But I quickly realized that I had explored a very, very small fraction of what this area had to offer. I've spent years exploring the Pacific Northwest and somehow managed to convince myself that I knew it pretty well. Turns out, I'd mostly been visiting the same places everyone else had. If I was going to build something that helped people discover new places, I should probably discover a few of those myself.
Being a Dork

Dork
noun
1. A stupid, inept, or foolish person
2. Someone who types `site:.gov filetype:pdf "hot springs"` into Google at 2 a.m. and feels powerful about it

What most people don't realize is that being a dork is a superpower. Search engines are tailored to give you what they think you need, not what you're actually requesting. But if you know a few secret commands, you can make search engines show you what you actually asked for.

There are many commands you can use, but here are a few of my favorites, and the most helpful. You might think that the more words the better, but sometimes it's better to leave things out on purpose. Using a dash, you can remove words or even entire sites.
`"hot springs" oregon -site:tripadvisor.com -"best of"`
This searches for pages that mention hot springs in Oregon, without returning pages from TripAdvisor or "best of" listicles.

On the other hand, how do you remember something you've forgotten? Sometimes you don't know the right word but still want to search anyway. Using a star, you can do just that. The star acts as a wildcard, returning all sorts of weird and wonderful goodies. Just make sure the whole phrase is in quotes, or Google will ignore it.
`"best * in Washington"`
This could return the best waterfalls, restaurants, hotels, cats, movies, all sorts of things. Use the dash from earlier to remove the ones you know you don't want.
If you have a budget for your adventure, that's an easy one too! Using two periods between two prices, you can search for a range.
`romantic dinner Seattle $50..$100`
Now that we know a few commands, we can narrow our search from hundreds of thousands of posts down to just a few that are most likely to have the information we're actually looking for.
`"romantic * in California" -"best of" $75..$150`

This should turn up pages talking about a "romantic picnic in California," a "romantic hike in California" or a "romantic weekend in California," minus the endless "best of" roundups, and only ones that mention a price somewhere between $75 and $150. What's left tends to be the good stuff: a small bed and breakfast's own website, a local blog post about a sunset sail, a winery's tasting menu. The kind of places that never make the top ten list, but probably should.
Fair warning: Google treats these more like suggestions than rules, so every once in a while it'll ignore you and do its own thing anyway. Even dorks don't win every time.
So what does all this dorking actually find? Here's one of my favorites. I was building out the Illinois pack and searched:
`illinois wacky fun indoor "things to do" $15..$50`

Somewhere past the usual lists of museums and deep-dish pizza, one result stopped me: a little arcade out in suburban Brookfield. Except it isn't little. It opened on Friday the 13th in 2010 with 130 games rescued from the scrap heap, and today it has more than a thousand, which makes it the largest video arcade in the United States. One door fee, and every single machine is on free play.
I had never heard of it. Most people I asked hadn't either. Now it's a mission: [Galloping Ghost Arcade](https://amblebee.com/missions/galloping-ghost-arcade/).
A dork found the dorkiest place in America. Honestly, that felt about right.
Finding the Balance

As it turns out, not everyone likes ~~paying to park in the middle of nowhere, wandering through the woods in the pouring rain, developing a deeply personal relationship with a blister, and climbing 2,000 feet to admire the inside of a cloud before enthusiastically recommending the experience to their friends~~ hiking.
This came as something of a surprise to me.

As I began building out the Oregon and Washington packs, I realized I had built a rather extensive catalog of ways to make your legs hurt. And worse, I had confused a well-rounded collection of adventures with a moderately aggressive fitness program.
I don't even like hiking.
I like waterfalls, mountain lakes, and standing somewhere that makes me feel incredibly small. Hiking just seems to be the inevitable inconvenience between the parking lot and the view.
And that got me thinking. Was I finding places worth experiencing, or was I just finding places that looked good in a photograph?
So how the duck do we actually balance these missions?

Well, what makes a balanced pack in the first place? Having just as many indoor missions as outdoor missions sounds reasonable, but does that make sense for a place like Hawaii? And while I'd love for every state to have a mission that takes you out into the desert, I think I'd be doing Vermont a disservice trying to find one. I don't know. I've never been to Vermont, but I'm about 60% confident there isn't a desert.
And what about price? Do we cater to those with hundreds of dollars to burn just for funsies, or do we exclusively look for things to do with the twenty dollars we found in last winter's coat?

How about time? Well, I work a full-time job and spend most of my weekends building AmbleBee. It's a little ironic that building a website encouraging people to get out of the house is largely responsible for me not getting out of the house. I don't always have a full day to explore, and sometimes an hour or two is all I've got.
And what about the time of year? A perfectly balanced pack in July might be a rather disappointing one in January.

Balance doesn't necessarily mean equal. It means that regardless of the weather, the amount of money in your pocket, the time of day, or who you're spending it with, there's a reasonable chance AmbleBee has something for you.

Trying to keep track of all that across fifty states, though, is a nightmare. At the time of writing, there are 603 mission files sitting in AmbleBee's repository, 224 of which haven't even made it onto the website yet. Somewhere in that enormous pile of ideas, I need to figure out what I have too much of and, more importantly, what I don't have enough of.
So, in classic fashion, I did what I always do when I need to do something smart but am too lazy to actually do it: I built another tool.

Mission Management gives me a rather colorful overview of every pack on AmbleBee. It looks at the balance between indoor and outdoor, inexpensive and pricier experiences, dates and adventures, things you can do in the winter, and things you can do after the sun goes down. I've already lost my mind, and I'm not particularly interested in having it leave me completely, so instead of trying to nail every pack perfectly, I gave it a little breathing room. As long as each pack is in the green, I'm happy.

One of my favorite features is the Gap Finder. Looking at it now, Louisiana is in desperate need of some attention. Only 12% of its missions are inexpensive, and nearly half of them have something to do with history. Now, I appreciate a good historical plaque as much as the next guy, but at some point I'd like to meet a gator.
Mission Management reckons that another eight inexpensive missions would bring that first number back into a comfortable range.

And just like that, my next research session has a purpose. I'm no longer sitting at my desk trying to find interesting things to do in Louisiana. I'm trying to find inexpensive things to do in Louisiana that don't involve being told to keep my voice down in a museum after a few too many daiquiris.
On my first trip to New Orleans, I had no idea those contained alcohol and may have inadvertently adopted them as my primary source of hydration.
Lovely place, New Orleans.
Anyway, back to the numbers.

And then there's the wonderfully colorful mess that is the theme coverage chart. Across the top are 42 different themes, everything from waterfalls and wildlife to arcades, architecture and small towns. Down the side are the packs. The darker the square, the more missions I've found for that theme.
It's the empty squares that tend to get me excited, though. Each one is a little reminder that there's probably something out there I haven't thought to look for yet.

Of course, the goal isn't to color in every square. I don't want to take away what makes each state interesting just to satisfy my insatiable need to make numbers look pretty on paper. Louisiana should feel like Louisiana, and Oregon should feel like Oregon.
The numbers are there to guide my curiosity, not replace it.
As it turns out, getting your ducks in a row is remarkably easy once you've built an entire system dedicated to the management of ducks.
The trouble is convincing someone to go see said ducks.
200 Words to Make You Go
Every mission gets about 200 words: one line to catch you, a paragraph to send you, and a little history to make you care.

The first part is the hardest. The short line has a hard limit of 100 characters, and not because I enjoy suffering. It's what shows up on the camera's tiny e-ink screen, so every mission has to fit in less space than a text message. Here's the short for Galloping Ghost:
Galloping Ghost Arcade near Chicago. Pay once and play hundreds of arcade games on free play.
Ninety-three characters, and I rewrote it about as many times.

If the short line is the handshake, the description is the pep talk. This is the part that has to get you off the couch. The description gets a little more room, up to 800 characters, because I'm not smart enough to write something interesting in just a few words, which is partially why these blog posts are so damn long.

I only have one rule here: tell people what to *do*, not what the place *is*. Anyone can read that Galloping Ghost has a thousand arcade machines. That's a researchable fact, not a plan. So the description hands you one:

Split up, each find the strangest game in the building, then bring the others back to play it. Finish with a head-to-head tournament on whatever game you argued about most. Get a photo of the group lit up by the screens.

And that last line isn't an accident. Every mission ends with something to photograph. Not "take some pictures," but something specific: the cliff at sunset, a selfie with the rock behind you, your whole crew glowing in the light of a thousand screens. The point of going out was never to tick something off a list. It's to come home with something worth keeping. And if you're like me and can never figure out what to take pictures of, that line helps a lot.

Galloping Ghost's description comes in at 445 characters, a little over half the limit. I've learned that the good ones rarely need all 800. If I'm running out of room, it usually means I'm explaining the place instead of sending you there.
Lastly comes the about, the little history to make you care. This one never goes near the camera. It only lives on the website, so it gets to slow down and tell you why this place is *this* place.
Galloping Ghost opened on Friday the 13th in August 2010 with 130 games rescued from the scrap heap...

Facts like that turn "an arcade" into a place with a story. Then there are the little things you'd never know to look for, like a spinning Sega R360 cabinet, one of only about a hundred ever made. Nobody needs to know any of this to have a good time. But it's the difference between playing some old games and saying, "Wait, come look at this."

Every mission also carries a pile of little labels. How long it takes: Galloping Ghost is a half day, because anything shorter and you'd be doing yourself a disservice. How much it costs: two dollar signs, enough to plan for but not enough to wince at. Whether it's indoors or out, whether it's a date, an adventure or both, who it suits, what time of day and what time of year. Is it a short drive, a day trip, or a "pack the car and tell your boss you're sick" kind of trip? Do you need to check opening hours or book tickets ahead of time?

None of that shows up as a paragraph, but all of it is quietly doing its job. It's what lets the **Filters** button find you a cheap, indoor, two-hour date on a rainy Tuesday. It's also exactly what Mission Management counts when it tells me Louisiana needs more inexpensive missions.

Then there are themes and tags. Themes come from a list of 42. I'd love to tell you that was a deliberate nod to *The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy*, but it was a happy accident, and the moment I add a 43rd, the joke's ruined anyway.

Each mission gets up to six. Galloping Ghost got three: games, quirky and playful. I'm not going to pretend it has anything to do with waterfalls. Tags are the loose words people actually type into a search bar, like "retro arcade" or "things to do near Chicago." It's the same dork energy from earlier, just pointed in the other direction. This time I'm trying to make sure *you* find *it*.

And when something about a place could genuinely ruin your day, it gets a caution right on the card: a road that turns into a four-wheel-drive track, a wash that floods in the rain, no cell service for miles. I learned that one the hard way, and you know how that story ends.
Which brings us to the part I'm *absolutely* never getting wrong again.
Finding the Pin
If you read the first post, you already know about the lake. Short version: one wrong digit shifted my lake pin four miles, and my phone gave up on navigation on the way home. I took it personally.

So now every pin gets the same treatment. I open the satellite view and ask one question: if I followed this pin with no signal and no idea where I was going, where would I end up? Not the middle of the park. Not the visitor center three miles from the trail. The actual place you'd park, the trailhead you'd start from, or the front door you'd walk through.

That usually means hopping between the park's own website, trail maps, street view and satellite view until they all agree. When they don't, it's usually the satellite view that helps me figure out why. Trees are remarkably unhelpful when questioned, but parking lots tend to give themselves away. Lakes, apparently, are another matter entirely.

Some pins only moved a few feet; some moved miles. A few early ones even had their latitude and longitude swapped, which is a fun way to send people to the wrong side of the planet. But since AmbleBee only covers missions in the US, that would no longer be our problem. (Just kidding.)
Every pin on AmbleBee has been checked by hand, and the ones still waiting don't go live until they have been. No more missing lakes. Probably.
When the Idea Comes From You
Remember way back at the beginning, when I said most missions start one of two ways: your suggestion or my insanity? Well, we've just spent a very long time on the insanity.

Once I've actually found a place, turning it into a mission takes me roughly an hour: writing the 200 words, tagging it, polishing it, and checking every fact and the pin. Some take less. Some take more, usually the ones where the lake has gone missing (again), the website hasn't been updated since 2009, and the only review is from a man named Gary who was "not impressed."
And that's not including the time it takes to find them!

With 379 missions live on AmbleBee (at the time of writing), that's somewhere around ~~me losing the rest of my very much needed sanity~~ 379 hours of writing and checking alone. That's more than nine full work weeks, or about sixteen straight days if you don't sleep. I mostly don't. And unlike a real work week, nobody's paying me for this one.

So when someone takes the time to send in a place they love, it means more than I can really put into words, which, given the length of this post, is saying something. You're not just saving me another trip down the rabbit hole. You're handing me ~~free labor~~ a place you've been to, or really want to go to. It mattered enough for you to share it, which means you're vouching for it, and that's surprisingly important!
Here's what happens when the idea comes from you.

There are two ways to send me a place. If you just want to point me somewhere, **Share an idea** takes under a minute: where it is and why you love it. If you've got the bug, or want to experience my insanity with me, **Build a mission** walks you through all the same fields I use: the short line, the description, the photo, the cautions, all of it. It's not as bad as I make it sound. What makes it bad is doing it for four hours straight at 11 p.m. Either way, you're welcome to skip the hard parts if you like. That's my job.

The second you hit send, you get a private link to follow along. You can watch your idea move from **Received** to **In review**, then **Working on it**, **Approved**, and finally **Live**. If I need something from you, like a better address or which trailhead you actually meant, the status changes to **We have a question**, and you can answer right there. Adding your email is optional, but it's the easiest way for me to reach you if your link ever goes missing.

Here's the part people don't expect: your idea goes through exactly the same process mine do. The same hour of writing and checking, the same pin hunt, the same rule: would I send my own family there? A suggestion doesn't get a shortcut, and that's on purpose. When a mission goes live, it carries the same promise, whether I found it at 2 a.m. or you did.

And if it makes it, it's yours! Tick the box and your name goes right on the mission. The first one that came from outside was [Pass-the-Canvas Sip and Paint](https://amblebee.com/missions/sip-and-paint/), a delightfully simple and very entertaining night, especially with a few daiquiris. It's one I'd never have thought of myself, mostly because my Mona Lisa is a stick figure jumping off a cliff. That mission is proudly credited to the friend who suggested it.

Not every idea makes it, of course. Some places have closed, some are on private land, and some just aren't quite a mission. When that happens, you'll get a real reason, not a form letter. (The ones that don't make it have a whole post of their own coming.)
Then a more recent suggestion taught me something about my own system, and it wasn't flattering.
Plugging the Holes

A friend sent in a great spot not long ago. Everything about it was right, and I was excited to tell them. Then I went back to write and realized something embarrassing: the only time my system let me send someone a message was when I was turning down their idea.

Approved? Silence. A quick question? Not really. A thank-you? Absolutely not. I'd built a front door that only opened to say no. Turns out, I'd gone to all the trouble of building a suggestion system and forgotten the basic principles of human conversation. Which tracks, considering I spend most nights locked behind a screen.

So I fixed it. Now there's one message box with a little menu: a question when I need more from you, a general note when I just want to say thanks or share an update, and a reason when something doesn't make it. And when someone builds a whole mission, the editor opens right beside their message, so I can shape it in their words, side by side. By the time it's a draft, it's mostly done, and it still sounds like the person who loved it first.

Of course, every system needs a safety net, because I'm still the guy who lost a lake. Before anything goes live, my little checkers (yes, I built even more tools) go over it one more time: the pins, the links, the Anywhere missions that need to work anywhere. Every mission shows when it was last checked, so you know how fresh it is. And if something's still wrong once it's out in the world, like a road closed or a business moved, there's a **Report a problem** button on every mission. Tap it, tell me what you found, and I'll fix it.
Which brings us to the most important part of a mission's life: yours.
Life After Launch
A mission isn't finished when it goes live. Honestly, that's when it starts. Everything up to this point has been me guessing what you'll love. After this, you get to tell me.

When you get home from a mission, tap **Mark done**. Give it a thumbs up or a thumbs down. That's it. One tap. It sounds small, but those thumbs are how I know which missions are worth making more of and which ones need a second look. A thumbs down isn't rude; it's useful. And if you've got a minute, tell me why. Don't pull a Gary. "Not impressed" doesn't help anybody. Some of my favorite fixes started with a thumbs down.

If you've got a little more to say, there's room for it right under the thumbs. Tell me what you loved or what didn't work. It's completely optional, and I only ask whether I can use it if you actually write something. If you say yes, I'll only ever quote you as "an AmbleBee user," never by name. And the personal note you keep for yourself stays yours. I can't see it, and I never will.

Every few missions, a stamp lands in your stamp book. Some mark milestones, some show up with the seasons, and a few are surprises I'm not going to spoil. Your profile keeps them safe on any device, with no name and no password. Just a private link that's yours.
But there are three stamps I hand out myself, one at a time:

items: Mission Maker, when a mission you suggested goes live
The Reporter, when a problem you reported gets fixed
Valuable Feedback, when something you told me actually changes AmbleBee

blocks.text: They're my way of saying thank you, because none of this works without you.
So, back to where we started. What do you do when you want to get out and experience something new, but can't think of anywhere to go?
Open a mission. Go do it. Go see the ducks. Then come back and tell me how it went.

posts.summary: A four-thousand-word explanation of how I populate a database
